Directions: Read the passage and then answer the questions that follow.
Context: A solar box cooker can be used to cook food or to purify water using light from the sun.
Title: Principles of Solar Box Cooker Design
Author: by Mark Aalfs
Content: The following heating principles will be considered `text(first)`:

:ibox:• Heat gain
• Heat loss
• Heat storage
A. Heat gain

`bbtext(Greenhouse effect)`: This effect results in the heating of enclosed spaces into which the sun shines through a transparent material such as glass or plastic. Visible light easily passes through the glass and is absorbed and reflected by materials within the enclosed space.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7a.jpg

The light energy that is absorbed by dark pots and the dark absorber plate underneath the pots is converted into longer wavelength heat energy and radiates from the interior materials. Most of this radiant energy, because it is of a longer wavelength, cannot pass back out through the glass and is therefore trapped within the enclosed space.
The reflected light is either absorbed by other materials within the space or, because it doesn't change wavelength, passes back out through the glass.
Critical to solar cooker performance, the heat that is collected by the dark metal absorber plate and pots is conducted through those materials to heat and cook the food.

`bbtext(Glass orientation)`: The more directly the glass faces the sun, the greater the solar heat gain. Although the glass is the same size on box `1` and box `2`, more sun shines through the glass on box `2` because it faces the sun more directly. Note that box `2` also has more wall area through which to lose heat.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7b.jpg

`ultext(Reflectors additional gain)`: `text(Single)` or multiple reflectors bounce additional sunlight through the glass and into the solar box. This additional input of solar energy results in higher cooker temperatures.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7c.jpg
B. Heat loss

The `text(Second)` Law of Thermodynamics states that heat always travels from hot to cold. Heat within a solar box cooker is lost in `text(three)` fundamental ways: `bbtext(Conduction, Radiation, and Convections)`.

`bbtext(Conduction)`: The handle of a metal pan on a stove or fire becomes hot through the transfer of heat from the fire through the materials of the pan, to the materials of the handle. In the same way, heat within a solar box is lost when it travels through the molecules of tin foil, glass, cardboard, air, and insulation, to the air outside of the box.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7d.jpg

The solar heated absorber plate conducts heat to the bottoms of the pots. To prevent loss of this heat via conduction through the bottom of the cooker, the absorber plate is raised from the bottom using small insulating spacers as in `bbtext(figure 6)`.

`bbtext(Radiation)`: Things that are warm or hot fires, stoves, or pots and food within a solar box cooker give off heat waves, or radiate heat to their surroundings. These heat waves are radiated from warm objects through air or space. Most of the radiant heat given off by the warm pots within a solar box is reflected from the foil and glass back to the pots and bottom tray. Although the transparent glazings do trap most of the radiant heat, some does escape directly through the glazing. Glass traps radiant heat better than most plastics.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7e.jpg

`bbtext(Convection)`: Molecules of air move in and out of the box through cracks. They convect. Heated air molecules within a solar box escape, primarily through the cracks around the top lid, a side oven door opening, or construction imperfections. Cooler air from outside the box also enters through these openings.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7f.jpg
C. Heat storage

As the density and weight of the materials within the insulated shell of a solar box cooker increase, the capacity of the box to hold heat increases. The interior of a box including heavy materials such as rocks, bricks, heavy pans, water, or heavy foods will take longer to heat up because of this additional heat storage capacity. The incoming energy is stored as heat in these heavy materials, slowing down the heating of the air in the box.
problems/MS22HSE2/media/S7g.jpg
These dense materials, charged with heat, will radiate that heat within the box, keeping it warm for a longer period at the `text(day's)` end.
